Title: Unbounded Loop in Background Celery Task Leads to Denial of Service (Resource Exhaustion)
Analysis:
### Vulnerability Analysis
The endpoint `/tasks/process` in `examples/celery/src/task_app/views.py` receives a user-supplied parameter `total` and parses it as an integer, then passes it directly to the Celery task `tasks.process.delay()`. In the Celery worker execution `examples/celery/src/task_app/tasks.py`, the `process` task iterates `total` times and sleeps for `1` second in each iteration. Since `total` is not bounded or validated, an attacker can supply an extremely large integer, causing the Celery worker thread/process to block indefinitely, leading to resource exhaustion and a Denial of Service (DoS) of the background worker pool.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
```http
POST /tasks/process HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:5000
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

total=99999999
```
This request will submit a background task that runs a loop 99,999,999 times, sleeping for 1 second each time (lasting over 3 years), exhausting worker processes and blocking all other background tasks.

Title: Insecure Direct Object Reference (IDOR) in Celery Task Result Retrieval
Analysis:
### Vulnerability Analysis
The endpoint `/tasks/result/<id>` in `examples/celery/src/task_app/views.py` retrieves the status and value of any Celery task by its ID without checking whether the requester is the owner of the task or has authorization to access it. An unauthenticated attacker can query the endpoint with a known or guessed task ID and obtain sensitive task details and results, leading to Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR).

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
```http
GET /tasks/result/8a719d36-3df5-46aa-b0c6-30291981fb5f HTTP/1.1
Host: localhost:5000
```
This HTTP GET request retrieves the execution results of the task with UUID `8a719d36-3df5-46aa-b0c6-30291981fb5f` from the database.

Title: Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) on State-Changing Endpoints in Tutorial Application
Analysis:
### Vulnerability Analysis
The blog deletion endpoint `/blog/<id>/delete` (and similarly other mutation endpoints like `/create` and `/update`) in `examples/tutorial/flaskr/blog.py` accept state-changing POST requests but fail to implement or validate Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) tokens. If a logged-in user visits a malicious website, the attacker's site can automatically submit a cross-origin form POST request to delete or modify the victim's blog posts, as Flask does not enable CSRF protection by default and the tutorial example code does not incorporate any anti-CSRF measures.

### Conceptual Exploit Payload
A malicious site can host the following auto-submitting HTML form to delete a post with ID 1:
```html
<form id="csrfForm" action="http://localhost:5000/1/delete" method="POST">
  <input type="submit" value="Submit">
</form>
<script>
  document.getElementById('csrfForm').submit();
</script>
```
When a victim who is logged into Flaskr visits this page, their browser automatically transmits their session cookie and executes the POST request, deleting post ID 1.
